---
title: "Maps"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.2, dpi = 100,
  fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", out.width = "100%"
)
options(gglaplot2.font = "inter")
library(ggplot2)
library(gglaplot2)
set.seed(2)
b <- gla_boroughs
b$share <- round(runif(nrow(b), 5, 40), 1)
b$change <- round(rnorm(nrow(b), 0, 4), 1)
```

`geom_gla_sf()` is `geom_sf()` with the house defaults: a `data-empty` fill,
a 1px `chart-surface` edge between areas and no graticule. `theme_gla_map()`
takes the axes away. The package carries the 33 London boroughs as
`gla_boroughs`; the sf package is needed to draw them.

## Outline

```{r outline}
ggplot(gla_boroughs) +
  geom_gla_sf() +
  gla_labs(title = "The London boroughs", source = "ONS Open Geography") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

## Your own figures

A table of figures by borough has to be joined to the boundaries before it
can be drawn. Load sf first: without it the boundaries are a plain table
with a column R cannot join or draw. Join on the code where the table has
one. Names work too, but have to match exactly, and `gla_boroughs` writes
them as the ONS does: "Barking and Dagenham", not "Barking & Dagenham".

```{r join}
library(sf)
figures <- data.frame(
  code = c("E09000007", "E09000012", "E09000033"),
  rate = c(4.1, 6.3, 3.8)
)
joined <- merge(gla_boroughs, figures, by = "code", all.x = TRUE)
head(joined[, c("name", "rate")], 4)
```

`all.x = TRUE` keeps every borough, so one with no figure is drawn in the
`data-empty` grey, not left out of the map. `dplyr::left_join(gla_boroughs,
figures, by = "code")` does the same. The boundaries go first in either:
the result is then still a map. `gla_boroughs` has 33 rows, the 32 boroughs
and the City of London, so a table of 32 leaves the City grey, and the
chart's note should say so.

## Choropleth

A sequential ramp for a quantity. The web maps draw it in steps, which
`scale_fill_gla_b()` does: a reader can match an area to a swatch in the
legend, labelled with the bin's range, which a smooth ramp does not allow.
`steps = 5` fixes the count at five bins of one rounded width, so it holds
as the data changes. `scale_fill_gla_c()` is the smooth form.

```{r choropleth}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = share)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b(name = NULL, steps = 5, labels = label_gla_percent(scale = 1)) +
  gla_labs(title = "A share by borough", subtitle = "Synthetic data for the example",
           source = "ONS Open Geography") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

## Change

A change calls for a diverging scale. `scale_fill_gla_b("diverging")`
counts its bins out from zero in equal steps, so zero is always a break,
and colours each side from the same ramp: one step below zero is as deep a
red as one step above is a blue. [Mapping a change](diverging-maps.html)
walks through one from the first draft to the finished chart.

```{r diverging}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = change)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL) +
  gla_labs(title = "A change by borough", subtitle = "Percentage points, synthetic data") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

When the change is lopsided, one large fall against small rises, the side
with fewer bins gets fewer, lighter steps. A smooth ramp would stretch its
darkest blue to the largest rise, however small, and put its neutral grey
at the middle of the data rather than at zero.

```{r lopsided}
b$lopsided <- b$change
b$lopsided[b$name == "Tower Hamlets"] <- -38
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = lopsided)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL) +
  gla_labs(title = "One borough has fallen far", subtitle = "Percentage points, synthetic data") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

To fix how many bins each side has, whatever the data does, set `steps`:
`steps = 3` is three below and three above, `steps = c(2, 4)` two and four.
Each side takes its own rounded step width, so the smaller side is not
stretched to match the larger.

```{r steps}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = change)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, steps = 3) +
  gla_labs(title = "Three steps each side", subtitle = "Percentage points, synthetic data") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

Where one area sits so far out that it takes the detail from the rest, set
`limits`. Values beyond them take the end step, which the legend then
labels "Below" its upper edge, and the chart should say which area it is.

```{r squished}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = lopsided)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, limits = c(-10, 10)) +
  gla_labs(title = "One borough has fallen far", subtitle = "Percentage points, synthetic data",
           note = "Tower Hamlets, at -38, is shown in the lowest step") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

`scale_fill_gla_c("diverging")` is the smooth form. Its neutral sits at
zero, or at `midpoint`, whatever the range of the data.

## Dark

```{r dark}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = share), theme = "dark") +
  scale_fill_gla_c(theme = "dark", name = NULL) +
  gla_labs(title = "A share by borough", subtitle = "On an inverse surface") +
  theme_gla_map(theme = "dark")
```

## Interactive

`gla_plotly()` turns the finished chart into an interactive one through
plotly. Each area's hover label is its name and its value, written as the
scale's `labels` write it and shown anywhere inside the boundary, and a
stepped scale converts as a legend. The name is the column called `name`,
or the one mapped as `aes(label = )` in `geom_gla_sf()`.
[Mapping a change](diverging-maps.html#interactive) has more on the label.

```{r interactive, eval = requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)}
gla_plotly(last_plot())
```
